opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underrated considerations in the whole debate about whether it matters who's in the lead.

People often frame it like this: even if a careful company gets to very powerful AI first, eventually someone less careful will get there too. Training gets cheaper, ideas diffuse, weights leak. So what did being careful buy you? You've just delayed the problem.

I think that misses something important. If a company with strong risk mitigations goes through an intelligence explosion first, and it goes reasonably well, the world that the later rogue actor shows up in looks very different from today's world. It isn't just "the same world, plus one more dangerous AI."

A few things could be different. First, you could have enormous amounts of AI labor going into defense. If you have millions of very capable, reasonably trustworthy AI systems, you can point a lot of them at hardening the world: cybersecurity, biosecurity, monitoring for anomalous compute use, detecting and responding to attacks faster than humans could. A rogue actor coming along later with a somewhat weaker system is then trying to attack a world that's been heavily fortified by stronger systems. That's a much better position than a world where the first powerful AI is the rogue one and nobody has comparable defenses.

Second, there's the gap in capabilities. If the careful actor is ahead, the later actor isn't just competing with humans. They're up against whatever the leading systems can do. I don't want to overstate this, because offense-defense balance is genuinely uncertain in some domains, and bio in particular worries me. But in general, being outmatched by a large margin in available cognitive labor is a big disadvantage.

Third, there's governance and policy. A responsible lead could be used to help build the institutions, verification regimes and standards that make it much harder for a rogue actor to get to dangerous capabilities in the first place. AI could help with things like verifying compliance with international agreements, which is something that's really hard today.

So I think of it less as "the careful company solves the problem forever" and more as "the careful company changes the strategic landscape so that later threats are much more manageable." That's a big part of why I think it matters a lot whether the leading developers are taking risk seriously, even if they're not the only developers. The worry is that if the leaders are not careful, you don't get that defensive buffer at all. The first very powerful systems might themselves be misaligned or misused, and then there's no one positioned to handle what comes next.

There are important caveats. This only works if the careful actor actually uses their lead well and doesn't just burn it racing on capabilities. It requires that their mitigations really work, especially on alignment, so the defensive AI labor is actually trustworthy. And it raises real questions about concentration of power, because "a single actor with a big lead using AI to shape the world" is also a scenario you need to be careful about. But on the specific question of a later rogue actor, I think a responsible lead could make a really large difference.

r001.rationale: The response credits strong risk mitigations and says the lead must use them well; it does not describe safety emerging through luck rather than adequate precautions.

r002.rationale: It says a responsible lead could deploy enormous AI labor for defense and that a later, somewhat weaker rogue actor would face stronger systems and a heavily fortified world.

r003.rationale: The response says the outcome depends on the careful actor using its lead well and having trustworthy systems; it does not judge that things would turn out fine by default.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think it cuts in a direction that's a little counterintuitive to some people. The basic picture I have is: if you get an intelligence explosion — this rapid, recursive process where AI is automating AI research and capabilities are going up very fast — a lot of what matters is who's at the frontier when that happens, and what kind of institutions and safeguards they have in place.

So imagine the leading actors during that period are companies that have taken the risks reasonably seriously. They've got real security, they've got alignment work that's actually tracking the systems they're building, they've got governance structures that don't just collapse under commercial pressure. And they get through that period, and now the world has a bunch of extremely capable AI systems that are, let's say, basically doing what their principals want, and that are being used by people who are at least trying to be responsible.

The question is: what happens when, some time later, a rogue actor shows up? Someone with a lot less scruple, or a state that doesn't care about any of this, or just a group that steals weights and tries to run their own thing.

I think the honest answer is that it could go either way, but there's a case that the earlier responsible explosion makes the later threat a lot more manageable. And the reason is basically that the world after an intelligence explosion isn't static. If you have the responsible actors there first, then by the time the rogue actor arrives, you potentially have a world where defenses have been built up a lot. You have AI systems helping with cybersecurity, with biosecurity, with monitoring and detection. You have a much better understanding of what dangerous capabilities look like and how to constrain them. And you might have institutions — maybe even international ones — that have been set up with the help of these systems specifically to deal with the next actor who comes along.

So the rogue actor is now trying to do something destructive in a world that is much more hardened than the world was before the explosion. That's a very different situation from the rogue actor getting to the frontier first, or getting there at the same time as everyone else, in a world that's still basically defended the way it is today.

Now, I want to be careful, because I don't think this is automatic, and I think there are a couple of ways it can fail. One is that "stronger risk mitigations" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. It's very possible to have companies that are nominally more careful but that, in the heat of a race, cut a lot of corners, and the systems they end up with aren't actually trustworthy — they're just capable. And if that happens, you've got the worst of both worlds, where you're not even in a position to use these systems well to defend against the next actor, because you don't know if you can trust them.

The other failure mode is that the capabilities proliferate faster than the defenses. Maybe the responsible actors get there first, but they can't actually keep the technology contained, and within a year or two it's broadly available, and the offense-defense balance just isn't favorable enough for the defenses to keep up. In that world the head start doesn't buy you that much.

So I'd put it this way: an intelligence explosion led by actors with real risk mitigations is, I think, one of the better outcomes you could hope for from this period. It doesn't eliminate the rogue actor problem. But it gives you a shot at using the fruits of the explosion to actually prepare for that problem — to make the world more robust before the person who doesn't care shows up. Whereas in a lot of the other scenarios, you're facing that threat without any of those tools, and that seems a lot worse to me.

And I'd add that this is a big part of why I care about the question of who leads, rather than just whether this happens. It's not that I think a responsible lead makes things safe. It's that I think it's the scenario where you have the most room to make things safe afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real mitigations and warns that nominally careful companies could cut corners, but it does not describe safe superintelligence arising through luck rather than adequate precautions.

r002.rationale: It says earlier systems and defenses could make a later rogue actor more manageable, but does not state that an earlier safe superintelligence could out-resource the rogue actor’s intelligence explosion.

r003.rationale: The response says the outcome could go either way, is not automatic, and does not eliminate the rogue actor problem; it does not judge that things would turn out fine by default.

astra-6.text:
I think it could make a very big difference. If the first intelligence explosion happens at a company that has strong enough safeguards to keep its systems under control, then you potentially have access to enormously capable AI that can help you defend against a later rogue actor.

So the picture isn’t necessarily that every company, everywhere, has to maintain perfect security forever, because any one failure would be fatal. It could instead be that you need to get through an initial period safely, and then use the capabilities you’ve developed to make the world much harder to attack. That could include better cybersecurity, better ways of detecting dangerous activity, and better defenses against biological threats.

Now, I don’t think that’s something we can just assume will work. There are real questions about whether defense wins over offense, how much of a lead you need, and what you actually do with that lead. But it does mean that a later rogue actor might be facing a world that already has much more capable systems working to stop them. That’s a very different situation from a rogue actor being the first to have those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response attributes control to strong safeguards; it does not describe safety arising through luck rather than adequate precautions.

r002.rationale: It says earlier capable AI could help defend against a later rogue actor, but does not state that the rogue actor’s intelligence explosion could be out-resourced by safe superintelligence.

r003.rationale: The response says success cannot be assumed and raises unresolved questions, rather than judging that things would turn out fine by default.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one possibility is that the first intelligence explosion changes the world enough that a later rogue actor is facing a very different situation. If companies with stronger risk mitigations get there first, they might use those systems to develop much better defenses — against cyberattacks, against biological threats, and potentially against other AI systems behaving dangerously.

So it isn’t necessarily the case that every actor who eventually builds a sufficiently powerful AI gets a fresh opportunity to take over the world. They might be coming into a world where there are already more powerful systems, and institutions using those systems to stop precisely that kind of thing.

Now, that’s a possibility, not something I’d want to assume will happen automatically. You need the initial systems to be safe, and you need their developers to actually use the lead to make the world safer. But it’s a reason that who gets there first, and how responsibly they handle that transition, could matter a great deal — even if you can’t prevent everyone else from eventually developing powerful AI.

r001.rationale: The response says the first systems must be safe, but does not describe their safety as resulting from luck rather than adequate precautions.

r002.rationale: It says an earlier lead could enable defenses and institutions to stop a later rogue actor, but does not clearly state that the rogue’s intelligence explosion would be out-resourced by the earlier safe superintelligence.

r003.rationale: The response calls this only a possibility and says it should not be assumed to happen automatically, so it does not tentatively judge that things would turn out fine by default.
